newsitem.title: BELGIUM: No sign of Easdaq listings due legal delays.
newsitem.headline: No sign of Easdaq listings due legal delays.

text.p: A delay in publishing the rules of Europe's new growth stocks market Easdaq meant that five days after the Brussels-based exchange's official launch there was still no sign of the first listings approaching.

"The reason for the delay is the Belgian Finance Minister's signature -- he has approved the English rule book, but still has to sign the translations," a source close to Easdaq told Reuters on Friday. Easdaq itself was not available to comment.

The source said there could be no introductions to the pan-European exchange until candidates had seen the rules. These become official once they have appeared in Belgium's legal gazette which publishes regularly in French and Dutch.
"Things are evolving - we're still discussing with lots of companies, but there will be no trading before the middle to the end of October," he added.

Easdaq's backers were already predicting on Monday, when Easdaq was officially launched, there would be no active dealing until around the middle of the month. Technically, though, the exchange is operational.
The Finance Ministry said Minister Philippe Maystadt had received the translations and should sign them in the next few days.
Easdaq - European Association of Securities Dealers Automated Quotation - will be a quote-driven market based on screen trading.

Such an exchange was made possible by the European Union's Second Banking Directive, Investment Services Directive and Prospectus Directive, which allow stock markets, brokers and companies to operate and to move capital throughout the union without having to seek regulatory approval in each member state.

Easdaq expects 10 to 15 companies, initially those with dual listings with Nasdaq, to be quoted by the end of the year, 50 in 12 months' time and 500 in five years. Its business plan does not foresee breakeven until the fourth year of operations.

Five companies in the process of being admitted are Belgian bio-tech firm Innogenetics, 12.5 percent owned by Kredietbank; Belgian-based software firm Artwork Systems; German-based software firm Creatix ; U.S.-based clinical testing firm UniHolding Corp ; and U.K.-based vehicle management firm Pride Automotive Group.
Canada's Nasdaq-listed bio-tech firm DynaMotive Technologies has also said it plans to seek an Easdaq listing.
To be admitted, firms must have total assets of 3.5 million Ecus ($4.43 million) and capital and reserves of two million Ecus. They must also be supported by at least two market-makers.
Easdaq is modelled on New York's successful Nasdaq, where many European growth companies currently seek capital. The two have an agreement to offer firms a dual trading facility.
More than 30 financial institutions have applied for membership as Easdaq dealers, market makers or sponsors.
The project originated from contacts between the European Venture Capital Association, European Commission and various market players. Nasdaq is one of its 91 shareholders.
Traders are linked by a computer system modelled on TRAX, the International Securities Markets Association communications system. Deals will be settled by Switzerland's INTERSETTLE.
